title: Handling the mushaf
hookLine: many keep it high, clean, and touch it only in wudu

cards: Look for the Qur'an in a Muslim family's home. You probably won't find it on the floor, under a pile of magazines, or on the bottom shelf beside the shoes.
It'll be up high, often wrapped in cloth, sometimes on a shelf by itself. A grandmother may kiss it before she opens it. A child may be told never to put anything on top of it.

teach.b: These customs come from how Muslims regard the Qur'an: the speech of God, written down. The written copy, the mushaf, is treated with the honor due to what it carries. One rule is about touching it.
Surah 56 describes the Qur'an, in Pickthall's words, as a book "Which none toucheth save the purified".
Scholars read that verse in more than one way; some commentators understand it to be about the preserved book in heaven, touched only by angels.

teach.h: THE SCHOOLS: TOUCH IT WITH WUDU
teach.b: Still, the four Sunni schools of law hold, as a rule, that a person should be in a state of purity, with wudu, to touch the Arabic mushaf.
They also point to a letter the Prophet ﷺ sent to Yemen, recorded in the Muwatta of Imam Malik: none should touch the Qur'an except one who is pure.
Some scholars held otherwise, and there are discussions about children who are learning, about translations, and about phones and apps, which some scholars say aren't a mushaf in the same sense.
Beyond the rules there's a whole culture of care. A folding wooden stand holds it open so it doesn't lie on the floor.

teach.h: A STAND, A HIGH SHELF, NOTHING ON TOP
teach.b: It often sits on the highest shelf, with nothing on top. People avoid taking it into a bathroom.

teach.h: WORN COPIES ARE BURIED, NOT TRASHED
teach.b: A worn-out copy isn't thrown in the trash: it's buried, or respectfully burned, or placed in special boxes that some mosques keep.
Some Muslims kiss it; others say no such practice is required, and simply handle it with care. What the customs share is simple: this isn't an ordinary book, so it doesn't get an ordinary place.

how: Many Muslims make wudu before touching the Arabic mushaf, keep it on a high, clean shelf with nothing on top, read it on a stand, and bury or respectfully dispose of worn-out copies.

games.why: in many homes it's kept high, clean and on its own: this isn't an ordinary book, so it doesn't get an ordinary place.

practice: If there's a mushaf or a translation in your home, picture where it sits right now, and whether it has a clean, high place with nothing stacked on it.
If you don't have one, think of the book or object you treat most carefully, and why, and notice what it feels like to honor something. If you pray, you might make wudu before you next open it.

wordCard.voice: Mushaf. The written copy of the Qur'an, handled with purity, a high place, and never the trash.
